The package drcTMB provides functions to fit dose-response curves using the Template Model Builder (TMB) framework.

## The drmTMB function

The main function in the drcTMB package is `drmTMB()`. There is some similarity to the `drm()` function from the drc package, with a simplified input of response and dose variables through a formula interface, and specifying a nonlinear model through the `model` argument. A full list of available models and their corresponding functions can be found at the end of this vignette.

Each of these models has the same parameter names, b1 for the lower and b2 for the upper asymptote, b3 for the steepness, b4 for the location of the inflection point on the dose scale, and b5 for an optional asymmetry parameter. The steepness b3 is positive for an increasing and negative for a decreasing curve. The asymmetry parameter b5 is estimated on a logarithmic scale. The models michaelismenten, asymptoticregression, and exponentialdecay have no steepness parameter; here b1 is the response at dose zero and b2 the asymptote at high doses. For the hormesis models braincousens and cedergreen, b5 is the size of the stimulation at low doses, see [Hormesis](#hormesis).
The `start` argument provides starting values for the parameters. The `fix` argument (TRUE/FALSE) allows to fix parameters at these starting values. Parameters that a model does not use, such as b5 for the Weibull models, are fixed automatically.

```{r}
library(drcTMB)
library(drcData)
data(ryegrass)
# Fitting a 3-parameter log-logistic model
mod <- drmTMB(rootl ~ conc, data=ryegrass, model="loglogistic", 
              start=c(0, 8, -1, 2, 0), fix=c(TRUE, FALSE, FALSE, FALSE, TRUE))
print(mod)
```

The model is fitted by maximum likelihood. For gaussian (and lognormal) models without random effects, the inference follows `lm()`, `nls()` and drc by default: the residual standard deviation is the square root of the unbiased residual variance with n - p residual degrees of freedom (`df.residual(mod)`), the standard errors are scaled accordingly, and confidence and prediction intervals use t quantiles. With `control = list(smallsample = FALSE)`, they use the maximum likelihood estimate and normal quantiles instead. The other families and models with random effects always use maximum likelihood and normal quantiles.

With the `predict()` method, we can visualize the fitted curve.
```{r}
newdata <- data.frame(conc = exp(seq(-0.5, log(30), length.out = 100)))
newdata$pred <- predict(mod, newdata = newdata)
library(ggplot2)
ggplot(ryegrass, aes(x = log(conc), y = rootl)) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_line(data = newdata, aes(x = log(conc), y = pred), color = "blue") +
  labs(x = "Log Concentration", y = "Root Length") +
  theme_bw()
```

### Confidence and prediction intervals

With `interval = "confidence"`, `predict()` adds standard errors and confidence intervals for the mean response, computed by the delta method. With `interval = "prediction"`, the intervals are for a new observation, adding the residual variation. The result is a data frame with the columns `fit`, `se.fit`, `lwr` and `upr`.
```{r}
# the controls (conc = 0) are drawn at a small concentration on the log axis
ryegrass$cplot <- ifelse(ryegrass$conc == 0, 0.25, ryegrass$conc)
ndata <- data.frame(conc = exp(seq(log(0.25), log(30), length.out = 100)))

ci <- predict(mod, newdata = ndata, interval = "confidence")
pri <- predict(mod, newdata = ndata, interval = "prediction")
head(ci, 3)

bands <- rbind(cbind(ndata, ci, interval = "95% confidence interval"),
               cbind(ndata, pri, interval = "95% prediction interval"))
ggplot(bands, aes(x = conc)) +
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = lwr, ymax = upr, fill = interval), alpha = 0.3) +
  geom_line(data = cbind(ndata, ci), aes(y = fit), colour = "blue") +
  geom_point(data = ryegrass, aes(x = cplot, y = rootl)) +
  scale_x_log10(breaks = c(0.25, 1, 3, 10, 30), labels = c("0", "1", "3", "10", "30")) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("steelblue", "grey60")) +
  labs(x = "Concentration (log scale)", y = "Root length", fill = NULL) +
  theme_bw() +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")
```

Alternatively, the intervals can be based on a parametric bootstrap of the model: `bootstrap()` simulates new responses from the fitted model and fits the model again to each of them. The bootstrap sample can be reused for the intervals of `predict()` and `confint()`.
```{r}
bs <- bootstrap(mod, nsim = 200, seed = 1)
head(predict(mod, newdata = ndata, interval = "confidence", boot = bs), 3)
```

### Model comparison

Nested models fitted to the same data can be compared by likelihood ratio tests with `anova()`, here the model with the lower asymptote fixed at 0 against a model with an estimated lower asymptote.
```{r}
mod4 <- update(mod, start = c(NA, NA, NA, NA, 0), fix = c(FALSE, FALSE, FALSE, FALSE, TRUE))
anova(mod, mod4)
```

For gaussian and lognormal models without random effects, F-tests account for the estimation of the residual variance with n - p residual degrees of freedom, as in drc, and are usually preferable for small experiments.
```{r}
anova(mod, mod4, test = "F")
```

A model without a dose effect, `model = "constant"` with the same mean b1 at all doses, tests whether the response changes with the dose at all, as `noEffect()` in drc.
```{r}
mod0 <- update(mod, model = "constant", start = NULL, fix = NULL)
anova(mod0, mod)
```

The chi-square distribution of the likelihood ratio statistic is only an approximation here, as the steepness and location of the curve are not identified under the constant model, and similarly for small experiments or for testing a standard deviation of random effects against zero. A parametric bootstrap test, `test = "boot"`, simulates responses from the smaller model and fits both models to each of them; with 200 simulations, the smallest possible p-value is 1/201.
```{r}
anova(mod0, mod, test = "boot", nsim = 200, seed = 1)
```

### Model diagnostics

The `plot()` method draws residuals against the fitted values and against the dose, and a normal QQ plot of the residuals. The default randomised quantile residuals are standard normal under the model for all families. A trend of the residuals against the dose points to a model function that does not fit the data, and `which = 4` adds QQ plots of the predicted random effects for models with random effects. The graphs are ggplot2 objects, returned invisibly, so a single one can be changed and drawn again.
```{r, fig.width = 7, fig.height = 6}
plot(mod)
```

## Effective dose estimation

The `ed()` function can be used to estimate effective doses (e.g., ED50, ED90) from the fitted model, given a specified response level (`respLev`). The effective dose ED p is the dose at which the response has changed by p% of the difference between the asymptote at low doses (the control) and the asymptote at high doses.
```{r}
(effdose <- ed(mod, respLev = c(25, 50, 75)))
```

Simultaneous confidence intervals can be constructed through the package multcomp. For gaussian models without random effects, the residual degrees of freedom of the model give multivariate t quantiles (`df.residual()` is `NULL` otherwise, and multcomp then uses the normal distribution).
```{r, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
library(multcomp)
linfct <- diag(3)
rownames(linfct) <- c("ED25", "ED50", "ED75")
effdose_glht <- glht(effdose, linfct = linfct, df = df.residual(mod))
confint(effdose_glht)
```

With `type = "absolute"`, `respLev` gives values of the response instead, and `ed()` estimates the doses at which the curve reaches them, here a root length of 2, 4 and 6 cm. These depend on the asymptotes as well, which is included in the standard errors.
```{r}
ed(mod, respLev = c(2, 4, 6), type = "absolute")
```

## Hormesis

Some toxic substances stimulate growth at low doses before the response declines. The hormesis models of Brain and Cousens (`model = "braincousens"`) and of Cedergreen, Ritz and Streibig (`model = "cedergreen"`) add a term $b_5\,g(x)$ to the response at dose zero in a log-logistic curve, with $g(x) = x$ or $g(x) = \exp(-1/x^\alpha)$; b2 is the response of the control, b1 the lower asymptote, and b3 < 0 for the decreasing curve. The exponent alpha of the cedergreen model is set by the argument `alpha` (1, 0.5 and 0.25 for the models CRS.a, CRS.b and CRS.c of drc). The hormesis effect b5 is on the scale of the response, and b5 = 0 is the log-logistic model, so `anova()` tests for hormesis. In the lettuce data, the plant weight increases at low concentrations of isobutyl alcohol.
```{r}
data(lettuce)
hmod <- drmTMB(weight ~ conc, data = lettuce, model = "braincousens")
hmod0 <- drmTMB(weight ~ conc, data = lettuce, model = "loglogistic", start = c(b5 = 0), fix = c(b5 = TRUE))
anova(hmod0, hmod, test = "F")
```

```{r}
lettuce$cplot <- ifelse(lettuce$conc == 0, 0.1, lettuce$conc)
hdata <- data.frame(conc = exp(seq(log(0.1), log(150), length.out = 100)))
hdata <- cbind(hdata, predict(hmod, newdata = hdata, interval = "confidence"))
ggplot(hdata, aes(x = conc)) +
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = lwr, ymax = upr), fill = "steelblue", alpha = 0.3) +
  geom_line(aes(y = fit), colour = "blue") +
  geom_point(data = lettuce, aes(x = cplot, y = weight)) +
  scale_x_log10(breaks = c(0.1, 1, 10, 100), labels = c("0", "1", "10", "100")) +
  labs(x = "Concentration (log scale)", y = "Weight") +
  theme_bw()
```

The effective dose ED p of a hormesis model is the dose above the peak at which the response has decreased from the control by p% of the difference to the lower asymptote, as in drc. It has no closed form and is found numerically; its standard errors follow from the implicit function theorem, also with random effects, and profile and bootstrap intervals are available as for the other models.
```{r}
ed(hmod, respLev = c(10, 50))
```

`peak()` estimates the dose at the peak of the stimulation and the maximal response, as `MAX()` in drc, with their joint covariance matrix, and `respLev = 0` gives the dose at which the response returns to the level of the control, the limit of the stimulation. Both are found numerically, with standard errors from the implicit function theorem as for the effective doses. Profile intervals are not available for the maximal response, and Wald intervals are given for it.
```{r}
(hpeak <- peak(hmod))
confint(hpeak)
ed(hmod, respLev = 0)
```

## Non-normal response distributions

The `family` argument allows to specify the distribution of the response as "gaussian", "lognormal", "poisson", "binomial", "beta", or, for overdispersed counts, the negative binomial "nbinom2" (variance mu (1 + mu/theta)) or "nbinom1" (variance mu (1 + phi)), and, for overdispersed binomial counts, the beta-binomial "betabinomial" with precision phi, as in glmmTMB. For the "lognormal" family, log(y) is normal around the log of the curve, which is then the median (geometric mean) of a positive response with a constant coefficient of variation, as in PROAST and the BMDS of the US EPA; the residual standard deviation is that of log(y), and the log-likelihood is that of y, so that AIC compares gaussian and lognormal fits.
To improve optimisation, the `link` argument allows us to estimate parameters on a transformed scale: a single link, e.g. `link="logit"`, applies to the asymptotes b1 and b2, and links named by parameter, e.g. `link=c(b1="logit", b4="log")`, to single parameters, with the defaults of the model for the others. The asymptotes have the identity (default), log or logit link. The log link for b4, `link=c(b4="log")`, is available for the models with a positive b4; random effects on b4 then vary the ED50 by a factor between groups, as in a logistic model of the log dose. The asymmetry b5 of the logistic and loglogistic models and the shape b5 of nec always have the log link. The parameters of the curves, e.g. b4 of each group or treatment, follow from `predict(fit, newdata, type="parameters")`, on their original scale or with `scale="link"` on the scale of the coefficients, with standard errors and confidence intervals. Furthermore, we can add constraints on the parameters through the `lower` and `upper` arguments with vectors for the lower and upper bounds of the parameters, respectively.

For the proportion of immobile daphnids after 48 hours, we fit a 2-parameter log-logistic model, with the asymptotes fixed at 0 and 1 and without asymmetry (b5 = 0). With only eight doses, the asymmetry parameter b5 cannot be estimated reliably: in a model with b5, the parameters b3, b4 and b5 are almost perfectly correlated, with very large standard errors.
```{r}
data(daphnids)
d48 <- subset(daphnids, time == "48h")

dmod <- drmTMB(cbind(no, total-no) ~ dose, data=d48, model="loglogistic", family="binomial", 
               start=c(0, 1, 1, 1000, 0), fix=c(TRUE, TRUE, FALSE, FALSE, TRUE))
dmod
```

The confidence intervals for the mean proportion are computed on the logit scale, so that they stay between 0 and 1. For the binomial, poisson and beta families, prediction intervals are quantiles of new observations, simulated at draws from the approximate normal distribution of the estimates (`nsim` draws). The number of trials of the new observations is taken from the response variables in `newdata`, here a new beaker with 20 daphnids at each dose; the value of `no` is not used.
```{r}
ndata <- data.frame(dose = exp(seq(3, log(22000), length.out = 100)), no = 0, total = 20)
cib <- predict(dmod, newdata = ndata, interval = "confidence")
pib <- predict(dmod, newdata = ndata, interval = "prediction", nsim = 2000, seed = 1)

ggplot(cbind(ndata, pib), aes(x = dose)) +
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = lwr, ymax = upr), fill = "grey60", alpha = 0.3) +
  geom_ribbon(data = cbind(ndata, cib), aes(ymin = lwr, ymax = upr), fill = "steelblue", alpha = 0.4) +
  geom_line(aes(y = fit), colour = "blue") +
  geom_point(data = d48, aes(y = no/total)) +
  scale_x_log10(breaks = c(100, 500, 2500, 10000)) +
  labs(x = "Dose (log scale)", y = "Proportion of immobile daphnids",
       subtitle = "Blue: 95% confidence interval; grey: 95% prediction interval for 20 daphnids") +
  theme_bw()
```

The simulated prediction intervals rely on the normal approximation of the estimates; for models with poorly identified parameters, a bootstrap sample (`boot = bootstrap(dmod)`) is the safer choice.


## Additional parameters

We can add covariates on the parameter level through the argument `fform`, with the parameters on the left-hand side of a formula, e.g. `b3 + b4 ~ 0 + time`, or a list of such formulas. Parameters that are not listed have a single intercept.

```{r}
# using the full daphnids dataset with groups 24h and 48h
dmodg <- drmTMB(cbind(no, total-no) ~ dose, data=daphnids, 
                model="loglogistic", family="binomial",
                fform=b3 + b4 ~ 0 + time,
                start=c(0, 1, 1, 1, 1000, 1000, 0), 
                fix=c(TRUE, TRUE, FALSE, FALSE, FALSE, FALSE, TRUE))
dmodg
```

```{r}
ndatag <- expand.grid(dose = exp(seq(3, log(22000), length.out = 100)), 
                      time = c("24h", "48h"))
ndatag$pred <- predict(dmodg, newdata = ndatag)

ggplot(daphnids, aes(x = dose, y = no/total, colour=time)) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_line(data = ndatag, aes(x = dose, y = pred, colour=time)) +
  labs(x = "Dose", y = "Proportion of Immobile Daphnids") +
  theme_bw() +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = c(100, 500, 2500, 10000), trans="log")
```


### Estimating effective doses for covariate values
The `newdata` argument of `ed()` specifies the dose-response curves by the values of the covariates in `fform`, one curve for each row; the effective doses are computed for each level of `respLev` and each curve.
```{r, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
(ed75 <- ed(dmodg, respLev = 75, newdata = data.frame(time = c("24h", "48h"))))

lfdiff <- rbind("24h"=c(1, 0),
                "48h"=c(0, 1),
                "48h-24h"=c(-1, 1))
edose_glht <- glht(ed75, linfct = lfdiff)
confint(edose_glht)
```

Ratios of effective doses, e.g. the relative potency of two curves, are often more natural than differences. As `ed()` returns the estimates and their variance-covariance matrix, simultaneous confidence intervals for ratios can be constructed with the function `gsci.ratio()` of the package mratios, here for the ED50 and ED75 after 24 hours relative to 48 hours.
```{r, eval=requireNamespace("mratios", quietly=TRUE)}
library(mratios)
ed5075 <- ed(dmodg, respLev = c(50, 75), newdata = data.frame(time = c("24h", "48h")))
num <- rbind("ED50 24h/48h" = c(1, 0, 0, 0),
             "ED75 24h/48h" = c(0, 0, 1, 0))
den <- rbind(c(0, 1, 0, 0),
             c(0, 0, 0, 1))
gsci.ratio(coef(ed5075), vcov(ed5075), num, den)
```

More generally, the `linfct` argument identifies the parameters b1 to b5 of each curve by linear functions of the model coefficients, with one matrix for each curve. The matrices for the two curves above are
```{r, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
linfct <- list("24h"=rbind(c(1, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0),
                           c(0, 1, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0),
                           c(0, 0, 1, 0, 0, 0, 0),
                           c(0, 0, 0, 0, 1, 0, 0),
                           c(0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 1)),
               "48h"=rbind(c(1, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0),
                           c(0, 1, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0),
                           c(0, 0, 0, 1, 0, 0, 0),
                           c(0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 1, 0),
                           c(0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 1)))
ed(dmodg, respLev = 75, linfct = linfct)
```

## Random effects

Fitting a 4-parameter log-logistic model to the vinclozolin dataset, which contains luminescence measurements of a dose-response experiment with 6 replications. The model includes correlated random effects for the lower and upper asymptote b1 and b2, with a random intercept for each replication. With only six replications, a model with an additional random effect for the location b4 cannot be estimated reliably. The `lower` argument is used to constrain the asymptotes and b4 to be positive, to improve optimisation. Random slopes are specified as in lme4, e.g. `rform = b4 ~ time | exper` for random intercepts and slopes of b4 in a covariate `time`; `ed()` then needs the value of the covariate in `newdata` to include the variation between replications in the standard errors.

```{r, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
data(vinclozolin)
vmod <- drmTMB(effect ~ conc, data=vinclozolin, 
               model="loglogistic", 
               rform=b1 + b2 ~ 1 | exper,
               start = c(b5 = 0), fix = c(b5 = TRUE), 
               lower = c(0, 0, -Inf, 0, -Inf))
summary(vmod)
```

We can visualise the predictions conditional on the random effects.

```{r, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
ndatav <- expand.grid(conc = exp(seq(-5, log(6), length.out = 500)), 
                      exper = levels(vinclozolin$exper))

# predict.drmTMB by default provides predictions conditional on the random effects
ndatav$pred <- predict(vmod, newdata = ndatav)
# prediction conditional on random effects = 0
ndatav$predpop <- predict(vmod, newdata = ndatav, random=FALSE)

ggplot(vinclozolin, aes(x = log(conc), y = effect, colour=exper)) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_line(data = ndatav, aes(x = log(conc), y = pred, colour=exper)) +
  geom_line(data = ndatav, aes(x = log(conc), y = predpop), 
            colour="black", linewidth=1.2) +
  labs(x = "log Concentration", y = "Fluorescence") +
  theme_bw() 

```

### Prediction intervals in a mixed-effect model

With random effects, the argument `random` decides which new observation a prediction interval is for. With `random = TRUE`, it is a new observation in the replication of each row of `newdata`, using its predicted random effects; the standard errors include the uncertainty of the predicted random effects. With `random = FALSE`, it is a new observation in a new replication, and the variance of the random effects is added. Rows of `newdata` with a replication that is not in the data are treated as new replications.
```{r, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
vinclozolin$cplot <- ifelse(vinclozolin$conc == 0, 0.01, vinclozolin$conc)
ndatav <- expand.grid(conc = exp(seq(log(0.01), log(6), length.out = 200)),
                      exper = levels(vinclozolin$exper))

# a new observation in each of the six replications
pic <- cbind(ndatav, predict(vmod, newdata = ndatav, interval = "prediction"))
# a new observation in a new replication
ndatap <- data.frame(conc = unique(ndatav$conc))
pin <- cbind(ndatap, predict(vmod, newdata = ndatap, random = FALSE, interval = "prediction"))

ggplot(pic, aes(x = conc)) +
  geom_ribbon(data = pin, aes(ymin = lwr, ymax = upr), fill = "grey60", alpha = 0.25) +
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = lwr, ymax = upr, fill = exper), alpha = 0.2) +
  geom_line(aes(y = fit, colour = exper)) +
  geom_line(data = pin, aes(y = fit), linewidth = 1) +
  geom_point(data = vinclozolin, aes(x = cplot, y = effect, colour = exper)) +
  facet_wrap(~ exper) +
  scale_x_log10(breaks = c(0.01, 0.1, 1, 5), labels = c("0", "0.1", "1", "5")) +
  labs(x = "Concentration (log scale)", y = "Fluorescence",
       subtitle = "Coloured: prediction interval in the replication; grey: in a new replication") +
  theme_bw() +
  theme(legend.position = "none")
```


### Estimating effective doses in a mixed-effect model

The `ed()` function is using the delta method to estimates effective doses and their corresponding standard errors. The standard error estimation includes by default the estimated variance components of the random effects. Here, the random effects are on the asymptotes only. The effective doses are defined relative to the asymptotes, so they do not depend on these random effects, and the standard error is the same as for the population curve. With a grouping variable in `newdata`, `ed()` computes the effective doses of the curves of fitted groups, conditional on their predicted random effects, e.g. `ed(vmod, newdata = data.frame(exper = "10509"))`.

```{r, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
(edv <- ed(vmod, respLev=50, random=TRUE))
```

We can additionally include the residual variance in the standard error estimation.
```{r, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
(edvr <- ed(vmod, respLev=50, random=TRUE, residual=TRUE))
```


## Benchmark doses

The benchmark dose (BMD) is the dose at which the response has changed from the response at dose zero by the benchmark response (BMR). Unlike an effective dose, it does not refer to the asymptote at high doses. The function `bmd()` offers the definitions `"excess"` (extra) risk, (p(BMD) - p0)/(1 - p0) = BMR, and `"additional"` (added) risk, p(BMD) - p0 = BMR, for proportions; the `"relative"` deviation from the response at dose zero, the default of EFSA for continuous responses; and, for gaussian and lognormal models without random effects, `"sd"`, a change by BMR residual standard deviations (of log(y) for lognormal, as in BMDS), the default of the US EPA for continuous responses without a biologically motivated BMR. The uncertainty of the estimated response at dose zero, and of the residual standard deviation, is included. The BMDL, the lower limit of a two-sided 90% interval, is the reference point of a risk assessment.

```{r, message=FALSE}
# 10% extra risk of immobility of daphnids
(bd <- bmd(dmod, bmr = 0.1, def = "excess"))
confint(bd, level = 0.9)

# ryegrass: a decrease of the root length by 5%, and by one standard deviation
bmd(mod, bmr = 0.05, def = "relative")
(bsd <- bmd(mod, bmr = 1, def = "sd"))
confint(bsd, level = 0.9)
```

EFSA recommends fitting both normal and lognormal responses. For the lognormal family, the curve is the median, and the relative BMD is that of the mean as well.

```{r, message=FALSE}
lmod <- drmTMB(rootl ~ conc, data = ryegrass, family = "lognormal", model = "loglogistic",
               start = c(b1 = 0, b5 = 0), fix = c(b1 = TRUE, b5 = TRUE))
AIC(mod, lmod)
confint(bmd(lmod, bmr = 0.05, def = "relative"), level = 0.9)
```

For the ryegrass data, the AIC clearly favours the normal distribution: the root lengths close to zero at high concentrations vary much more on the log scale. The BMDs of the two fits differ considerably, which shows how much the BMD can depend on the assumed distribution.

With random effects, the BMD can refer to two different curves: the typical curve, with the random effects at zero (`scale = "conditional"`), or the marginal mean curve, the mean response of the population of groups (`scale = "marginal"`, the default), found by integrating the curves over the distribution of the random effects. Both are the same if the random effects enter the mean linearly, as random effects on the asymptotes with the identity link in the vinclozolin model; random effects on b4 or b3, or on asymptotes with a log or logit link, make them differ. The standard errors of marginal BMDs include the uncertainty of the variances of the random effects. Profile intervals are not available for marginal BMDs that need the integration; `confint()` then returns Wald intervals, and `method = "boot"` bootstrap intervals.

```{r, message=FALSE}
bmd(vmod, bmr = 0.1, def = "relative")
```

The continuous models of PROAST and BMDS include the exponential and power models, which have no upper asymptote: `model = "exponential"`, $b_1 \exp(b_4 x^{b_3})$, and `model = "power"`, $b_1 + b_4 x^{b_3}$, with the response $b_1$ at dose zero, the power $b_3 > 0$, and the coefficient $b_4$, negative for a decreasing curve. Fixing the power at 1 gives the exponential model 2 (exp2), and estimating it exp3. For the ryegrass data, the power is needed, but the log-logistic model fits better.

```{r, message=FALSE}
emod2 <- drmTMB(rootl ~ conc, data = ryegrass, model = "exponential",
                start = c(b3 = 1), fix = c(b3 = TRUE))
emod3 <- drmTMB(rootl ~ conc, data = ryegrass, model = "exponential")
anova(emod2, emod3)
AIC(mod, emod3)
confint(bmd(emod3, bmr = 0.05, def = "relative"), level = 0.9)
```

### Model averaging

The BMD can depend considerably on the dose-response model and the distribution, as for the normal and lognormal fits of the ryegrass data above. Instead of selecting one model, `bmdma()` averages over several models fitted to the same data, with AIC weights, as recommended by EFSA (2017), or BIC weights (`weights = "BIC"`), which favour simpler models. With `average = "curve"` (the default), the BMD is that of the averaged curve, the AIC-weighted mean of the fitted curves; with `average = "bmd"`, the AIC-weighted mean of the BMDs of the models. The BMDL is the lower limit of a bootstrap percentile interval: each bootstrap sample is simulated from a model drawn with its weight, all models are fitted to it, and the weights and the averaged BMD are computed again. Lognormal models get the weight zero in samples with non-positive responses.

```{r, message=FALSE}
wmod <- drmTMB(rootl ~ conc, data = ryegrass, model = "weibull1",
               start = c(b1 = 0, b5 = 0), fix = c(b1 = TRUE, b5 = TRUE))
w2mod <- drmTMB(rootl ~ conc, data = ryegrass, model = "weibull2",
                start = c(b1 = 0, b5 = 0), fix = c(b1 = TRUE, b5 = TRUE))
(ma <- bmdma(LL = mod, W1 = wmod, W2 = w2mod, LLlognormal = lmod, bmr = 0.05,
             def = "relative", nsim = 200, seed = 1, progress = FALSE))
```

For `average = "bmd"`, `confint(ma, method = "buckland")` gives Wald intervals with the standard error of Buckland et al. (1997), which combines the standard errors of the models with the spread of their BMDs, without a bootstrap.


### Model functions

All models except exponential and power are of the form $f(x) = b_1 + (b_2 - b_1) F(x)$, with a function $F$ increasing from 0 to 1. For the models with steepness parameter $b_3$, $b_1$ is the lower and $b_2$ the upper asymptote, and the curve is increasing for $b_3 > 0$ and decreasing for $b_3 < 0$.

#### logistic

$$ f(x) = b_1 + \frac{b_2 - b_1}{\left( 1 + \exp \left( -b_3 \left( x - b_4 \right) \right) \right)^{\exp(b_5)}} $$

#### loglogistic

$$ f(x) = b_1 + \frac{b_2 - b_1}{\left( 1 + \exp \left( -b_3 \left( \log(x) - \log(b_4) \right) \right) \right)^{\exp(b_5)}} $$

#### weibull1

$$ f(x) = b_1 + \left( b_2 - b_1 \right) \exp \left( -\exp \left( -b_3 \left( \log(x) - \log(b_4) \right) \right) \right) $$

#### weibull2

$$ f(x) = b_1 + \left( b_2 - b_1 \right) \left( 1 - \exp \left( -\exp \left( b_3 \left( \log(x) - \log(b_4) \right) \right) \right) \right) $$

#### lognormal

$$ f(x) = b_1 + \left( b_2 - b_1 \right) \Phi \left( b_3 \left( \log(x) - \log(b_4) \right) \right) $$

where $\Phi (\cdot)$ is the cumulative distribution function of the standard normal distribution.

#### gompertz

$$ f(x) = b_1 + \left( b_2 - b_1 \right) \exp \left( -\exp \left( -b_3 \left( x - b_4 \right) \right) \right) $$

#### braincousens

A hormesis model; b2 is the response at dose zero, b1 the lower asymptote at high doses, and b5 the size of the stimulation at low doses. The curve returns to b1 at high doses for $b_3 < -1$.

$$ f(x) = b_1 + \frac{b_2 - b_1 + b_5 x}{1 + \exp \left( -b_3 \left( \log(x) - \log(b_4) \right) \right)} $$

#### cedergreen

A hormesis model as braincousens, with a fixed exponent $\alpha$ (argument `alpha`).

$$ f(x) = b_1 + \frac{b_2 - b_1 + b_5 \exp \left( -1/x^{\alpha} \right)}{1 + \exp \left( -b_3 \left( \log(x) - \log(b_4) \right) \right)} $$

#### michaelismenten

For the following models without steepness parameter, $b_1$ is the response at dose zero and $b_2$ the asymptote at high doses.

$$ f(x) = b_1 + \frac{b_2 - b_1}{1 + \frac{b_4}{x}} $$

#### gamma

As michaelismenten, with the distribution function of the gamma distribution with shape $b_3 > 0$, $P(\cdot, b_3)$; the gamma model of BMDS for quantal responses, with $b_1$ the background risk and $b_2$ fixed at 1. With $b_3 = 1$, it is the asymptoticregression model.

$$ f(x) = b_1 + \left( b_2 - b_1 \right) P \left( \frac{x}{b_4}, b_3 \right) $$

#### multistage

The multistage model of BMDS, with the coefficients $\beta_1$ to $\beta_3$ of its polynomial in $b_3$ to $b_5$, bounded below by 0 by default; for quantal responses, $b_1$ is the background risk and $b_2$ is fixed at 1. Fixing $b_5$ at 0 gives the model of degree 2, and fixing $b_4$ and $b_5$ at 0 the model of degree 1, which is the asymptoticregression model with $b_4 = 1/\beta_1$. The model of degree 2 with $b_1 = 1$ and $b_2 = 0$ is the linear-quadratic model of radiobiology, $S = \exp(-\alpha x - \beta x^2)$, with $\alpha = b_3$ and $\beta = b_4$.

$$ f(x) = b_1 + \left( b_2 - b_1 \right) \left( 1 - \exp \left( -b_3 x - b_4 x^2 - b_5 x^3 \right) \right) $$

#### nec

The threshold model, with no effect up to the no-effect concentration $b_4$: $b_1$ is the response up to the threshold, $b_2$ the asymptote at high doses, $b_3 > 0$ the rate and $b_5$ the shape on the log scale, with $(x - b_4)_+ = \max(x - b_4, 0)$. With $b_5 = 0$, it is the NEC model of drc; with $b_5 > 0$, the curve is sigmoidal above the threshold. With random effects on $b_4$, the threshold is smoothed by default, replacing $(x - b_4)_+$ by $s \log(1 + \exp((x - b_4)/s))$ with a width $s$ of 0.1 times the smallest interval between the doses (argument `smooth`).

$$ f(x) = b_1 + \left( b_2 - b_1 \right) \left( 1 - \exp \left( -\left( b_3 (x - b_4)_+ \right)^{\exp(b_5)} \right) \right) $$

#### haldane

The substrate inhibition model of Haldane, as michaelismenten with the inhibition $b_5 = 1/K_i \geq 0$ (bounded below by 0 by default): $b_2$ is the maximal response without inhibition ($V_{max}$) and $b_4$ the half-saturation constant ($K_m$). With $b_5 = 0$, it is the michaelismenten model, so that `anova()` tests for inhibition. The curve has its peak at $x = \sqrt{b_4/b_5} = \sqrt{K_m K_i}$, given with its standard error by `peak()`; effective doses are not defined.

$$ f(x) = b_1 + \frac{(b_2 - b_1) x}{b_4 + x + b_5 x^2} $$

#### asymptoticregression and exponentialdecay

Both names refer to the same model; an increasing curve is an asymptotic regression and a decreasing curve an exponential decay.

$$ f(x) = b_1 + \left( b_2 - b_1 \right) \left( 1 - \exp \left( \frac{-x}{b_4} \right) \right) $$

#### exponential and power

The exponential and power models of PROAST and BMDS have no upper asymptote: $b_1$ is the response at dose zero, $b_3 > 0$ the power (bounded below by 0 by default) and $b_4$ the coefficient, whose sign gives the direction of the curve; $b_2$ and $b_5$ are not used. Fixing $b_3$ at 1 gives the exponential model 2 (exp2) of PROAST and BMDS, and the exponential model with $b_3$ estimated is exp3. Relative effective doses are not defined; `ed(type = "absolute")` and `bmd()` give absolute effective doses and benchmark doses.

$$ f(x) = b_1 \exp \left( b_4 x^{b_3} \right) \qquad f(x) = b_1 + b_4 x^{b_3} $$

#### constant

A model without a dose effect, for testing a dose-response model against a flat curve with `anova()`; b2 to b5 are not used.

$$ f(x) = b_1 $$
